titre: Sweden Abolishes the King's Prior Review of Writings in 1766, but Not the Church's
accroche: In 1766, Sweden enacts the ordinance regarded as the first press freedom law, yet it keeps prior review by the Church.
contenu_vulgarise:
On December 2, 1766, Sweden enacts an ordinance on freedom of the press. The Library of Congress says it is “regarded” as the world's first press freedom law, and the Swedish National Archives present it as the first of its kind. The label deserves some precision: what did this text actually free, and what did it leave under control?

## The King's Prior Censorship Disappears

The first codified censorship rules in Sweden date from 1661: two copies of every book printed in the kingdom had to be sent to the royal office for review. The 1766 ordinance abolishes all prior review by the king. It also sets out a principle of broader scope than the mere right to print: Article 10 provides free access to all archives, in order to make copies or obtain a certified copy. The Library of Congress sees in it the first law to establish citizens' access to public documents.

The Library of Congress reports that the ordinance has been described as drafted by a Finn, Anders Chydenius, a pastor and member of the Swedish Parliament. The Swedish National Archives see him as a “driving force” behind the text. Finland is part of Sweden until 1809.

## What Remains Forbidden

The text does not end all surveillance. Writings concerning the Lutheran faith remain subject to prior review by the Church, and writings contrary to that faith are punished by a fine of 3,000 silver daler. Other subjects are off-limits: the power, rank, and relations of the king, contemptuous remarks about members of Parliament, and the defamation of private individuals. Outside these limits, the Library of Congress sums up, everything not expressly prohibited is permitted.

The list deserves a close reading. It protects the official faith, the king, and Parliament, that is, the powers that be, as much as private individuals. The fine of 3,000 silver daler, which the Library of Congress values at about $2,200 in today's money, is attached to writings contrary to the Lutheran faith. Through its Article 10, the ordinance also opens up to citizens the archives, that is, the documents those powers produce.

## What This Changes

This story is often told as one of absolute freedom arriving too early. The text says something else: a freedom defined by precise exceptions, some of which, like religion, remain broad enough to weigh on what the press can say. Nor should it be read as a lasting conquest. According to the Library of Congress, the ordinance was considered to have constitutional status until 1772, the year Gustav III begins to concentrate power in his office, until he becomes the sole legislator. It regains its importance in 1809, in the constitutional reform that incorporates it, amended, into the new Constitution.

The question remains, then, of what matters most in a law of freedom: the principle it affirms, or the list of cases it excepts.

repere.texte: December 2, 1766: Sweden abolishes prior review by the king, keeps review by the Church for writings on the Lutheran faith, sets a fine of 3,000 silver daler for a writing contrary to that faith, and opens access to public archives through its Article 10.
repere.source: Library of Congress, Law Library, “250 Years of Press Freedom in Sweden,” 2016

carte.punch: In 1766, Sweden ends the king's prior censorship but keeps review of religious writings.
carte.idee: Sweden's ordinance of December 2, 1766 abolishes prior review by the king and opens access to public archives. It maintains review by the Church of writings on the Lutheran faith and a fine of 3,000 silver daler against those who contradict it.

quiz.question: What does Sweden's 1766 ordinance keep despite the end of prior censorship?
choix: Prior control by the king over all political writings
Review by the Church of writings concerning the Lutheran faith
A requirement of Parliament's authorization for every printer
Prior review by the Church of all writings, whatever their subject
quiz.explication: The Library of Congress writes that the ordinance abolishes all prior review by the king and requires only that of the Church, for matters of Lutheran faith. The other forbidden subjects (the king, members of Parliament, private individuals) are content limits: the source mentions neither parliamentary authorization for printers nor review by the Church of all writings.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Article 10 of the 1766 ordinance allow?
choix: Free access to public archives, to make copies or obtain a certified copy
The right to publish without ever citing one's sources
Direct election of members of Parliament by newspaper readers
The abolition of the fine for writings contrary to the Lutheran faith
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Article 10 of the 1766 ordinance opens to citizens free access to the archives, to make copies or obtain a certified copy, according to the Library of Congress. Nothing in it concerns citing sources, electing Parliament, or the religious fine.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happens to the status of the 1766 ordinance in 1772?
choix: The Swedish Parliament repeals it after a unanimous vote
The Church gains the right to censor political writings as well
Gustav III concentrates power and becomes the sole legislator
Finland separates from Sweden and keeps its own version of the text
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Library of Congress writes that the ordinance had constitutional status until 1772, the year Gustav III begins to concentrate power in his office, until he becomes the sole legislator. Neither repeal, political censorship, nor Finnish separation is mentioned.
